title: TemplateLeak: A Template-Disjoint Evaluation Audit of CommonForms Form Field Detection

raw.stage1:
**Purpose:**  
The contribution's purpose is to provide a principled way to test whether template overlap between train/test splits inflates detection metrics in document understanding benchmarks. Paper [3] discusses the importance of reporting train-test overlap for language models, but it does not propose a method to test the inflation of detection metrics due to template overlap. Paper [4] addresses benchmark leakage in LLMs but focuses on detecting leakage rather than testing its impact on metrics. Paper [5] highlights issues with train-test splits in protein interaction benchmarks but does not address template overlap or its metric inflation effects. None of the prior papers establish the same objective of testing metric inflation due to template overlap in document understanding benchmarks.  

**Mechanism:**  
The contribution introduces the TemplateLeak audit framework, which combines MinHash/LSH clustering of form pages by field-layout similarity with document-level permutation testing. Papers [2], [6], [8], and [26] all discuss MinHash and LSH techniques for detecting near-duplicate documents or similarity, which is substantively equivalent to the clustering mechanism used here. Papers [12], [13], [20], [25], and [27] discuss permutation tests for statistical significance, which is substantively equivalent to the permutation testing mechanism used here. Thus, the mechanism is covered by these prior works.  

**Evaluation:**  
The evaluation involves applying the framework to CommonForms, partitioning the test set into Overlap-Test and Novel-Test slices, and running a 1000-permutation null test. Papers [12], [13], [20], [25], and [27] describe permutation testing as a statistical validation method, which matches the evaluation design here. While the specific dataset (CommonForms) and partitioning are new, the evaluation design itself (permutation testing) is covered.  

**Domain:**  
The contribution operates in the domain of form field detection/document understanding benchmark auditing. Papers [4], [5], [18], and [19] address benchmark auditing in other domains, such as LLMs, protein interaction benchmarks, and virtual screening models. These papers demonstrate that benchmark auditing is an established application area, even though the specific focus on form field detection is new. The domain is therefore covered.  

**Verdicts:**
